records.title: Why do some emergency departments deliver sepsis bundles reliably? A multi-site qualitative study using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research
records.authors: Nakamura-Obi E, Lindqvist-Mensah R, Carvalho-Doyle P
records.abstract: We interviewed 58 staff in six emergency departments, three with consistently high and three with low rates of antibiotics within one hour for suspected sepsis, and coded the interviews with the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. High-performing departments had nurse-initiated antibiotic protocols, a sepsis champion on every shift and antibiotics stocked near triage. Low-performing departments relied on physician orders, described crowding and handover delays, and kept antibiotics in a pharmacy room away from triage. Staff at all sites knew the bundle well. Night shifts were described as the weakest point in low performers, where one physician covered the whole department.

records.title: Variation in time to antibiotics for sepsis across a regional hospital network: a benchmarking report
records.abstract: This report compares time to antibiotics for adults with suspected sepsis across nine hospitals in one regional network over twelve months. The proportion of patients receiving antibiotics within one hour of recognition ranged from 41 to 86 percent between hospitals. In every hospital the proportion was lower at night and at weekends, and the gap between day and night was largest in the smaller hospitals. Hospitals differed in how recognition time was recorded, which limits comparison. The report does not examine reasons for the variation and recommends that hospitals with lower figures learn from those with higher figures.

records.title: What helps and hinders timely sepsis bundle delivery in hospitals: a systematic review of 27 qualitative and mixed-methods studies
records.authors: Adeyemi-Fairclough T, Borg-Haddad N, Sato-Keane L
records.abstract: We synthesised 27 qualitative and mixed-methods studies of sepsis bundle delivery in hospitals. Across 27 studies, the most consistent barriers were crowding, unclear responsibility for ordering antibiotics and delayed access to antibiotics, and the most consistent facilitators were protocols allowing nurses to start treatment, visible leadership and regular feedback of performance. Confidence in these findings, assessed with GRADE-CERQual, was moderate for most themes and low for leadership. Few studies compared high- and low-performing sites directly, and night-time care was rarely examined separately. The authors recommend comparative designs that explain variation between sites.

records.title: Nurse-initiated sepsis protocols and time to antibiotics: a stepped introduction across four emergency departments
records.abstract: Four emergency departments introduced a protocol allowing triage nurses to start antibiotics for suspected sepsis, one department every three months. Across the four departments, median time from triage to antibiotics fell from 94 to 58 minutes after the protocol started. The fall was greatest in departments where pharmacy stocked antibiotics in the emergency department, and smallest where nurses reported low confidence in using the protocol without a physician present. Night-time performance improved less than daytime performance. The introduction was not randomised and other changes happened at the same time, so the size of the effect is uncertain.

response.synthesis: Four retrieved records, a small yield. A multi-site study and a review of 27 studies agree on the main determinants: nurse-initiated protocols, a champion on every shift, antibiotics stocked near triage, leadership and feedback help; crowding, unclear responsibility for ordering and distant antibiotic stock hinder. Variation between hospitals of the size described locally is common and is worse at night. Few studies compare high and low performers directly or examine night care, which is what this question needs.
response.gradeRationale: Qualitative evidence from a multi-site study and a review with GRADE-CERQual ratings mostly moderate, consistent across settings; the quantitative records are non-randomised or descriptive. Moderate confidence in the main determinants; low for night-time care.
response.summary: Four retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded; overall certainty moderate for the determinants.

response.reading: Timely antibiotics depend on who may start them, how close they are to triage, whether someone owns sepsis on each shift, and how crowded the department is; the same bundle performs differently where these differ. Night shifts concentrate the weaknesses. The network's figures can select contrasting sites, and staff accounts can explain the contrast.

response.rationale: The question is why delivery differs between sites, which staff accounts and observation can explain and performance figures cannot. A multi-site qualitative study, with sites contrasted by network time-to-antibiotics figures (c2) and interviews and observation coded with CFIR starting from known determinants (c1, c3), identifies what an implementation strategy should target. Testing a strategy now would be premature because the local determinants are unknown.

response.title: Why sepsis bundle delivery differs between hospitals: a multi-site qualitative study of higher- and lower-performing sites
response.abstract: Objective: to identify determinants of timely antibiotic delivery for sepsis that distinguish higher- from lower-performing hospitals, by day and at night. Design: multi-site qualitative study at five hospitals with staff interviews and structured observation, coded with CFIR. Results and conclusions will be written after analysis.
response.introduction: Variation in time to antibiotics for sepsis between hospitals is common and worse at night, yet few studies explain it by comparing sites directly.
response.methods: Sites were contrasted using network figures. About 8 to 10 staff per site were interviewed and one day and one night shift observed. Summaries were coded with CFIR, constructs were rated by site, and higher- and lower-performing sites were compared.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present constructs by site, the high-low contrast and night-care findings.
response.discussion: The discussion will relate the determinants to strategies such as nurse-initiated protocols and antibiotic stock at triage, and state what the network should test next.
response.limitations: Staff accounts; five sites in one network; no patient interviews.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will name determinants, not claim effects of any strategy.
